name: Tibetan ache lhamo opera
lineage: Tibetan ache lhamo ("sister-goddess") folk-opera tradition. Origin traced by tradition to the fourteenth-century yogi-engineer-saint Thangtong Gyalpo, who is said to have founded the form and organized the first performance-troupe to raise funds for his iron-chain suspension-bridge construction projects across Tibet. The canonical repertoire comprises eight classical plays drawn from Indo-Tibetan Buddhist narrative cycles, including Sukyi Nyima (the deer-girl), Drowa Sangmo (the celestial-bride), Chöyi Nyima, Pema Wöbar, Drimé Künden, Nangsa Wöbum, Gyasa Belsa, and Donyö Dondrup. Performance integrates singing (with distinctive named melodic-modes), stylized dance-and-mime movement, recited dialogue, and percussion accompaniment (rolmo large paired cymbals and damaru double-headed hand-drum the principal instruments — no melodic instruments, the form is essentially voice-and-percussion). The Lhasa-region Kyumolung style and the Shang and Gyenpa regional styles constitute the three main lineages. Performance traditionally outdoors during summer festivals, particularly the Shotön (yogurt-festival) at Norbulingka in Lhasa. The Tibetan Institute of Performing Arts (TIPA, Dharamshala, India) maintains the principal exile-community transmission lineage post-1959. Distinguished from the parallel monastic-liturgical yang chant by ache lhamo's secular-narrative (vs liturgical) functional framework and absence of long-trumpets and double-reed monastic-ensemble instrumentation; distinguished from Chinese jingju by Tibetan-language repertoire and characteristic voice-and-percussion-only ensemble configuration.
